title: Old Fezziwig's Ball
text:
In A Christmas Carol, the Ghost of Christmas Past takes Ebenezer Scrooge back to the warehouse where he served his apprenticeship as a young man. There sits his old master, Fezziwig, a kindly old gentleman in a Welsh wig.

It is seven o'clock on Christmas Eve. Fezziwig calls out cheerfully to young Scrooge and his fellow apprentice Dick Wilkins: no more work tonight. The shutters go up, the floor is swept, the lamps are trimmed, and the warehouse turns into a ballroom. A fiddler arrives. In come Mrs. Fezziwig and the three Miss Fezziwigs, their young admirers, all the young people employed in the business, the housemaid, the baker, the cook. There is dancing, cake, roast, mince pies and plenty of beer, and Fezziwig and his wife dance with such energy that they seem to shine. At eleven the ball breaks up, and the Fezziwigs shake hands with every guest at the door.

The Ghost remarks that it was a small matter: Fezziwig spent only a few pounds. Scrooge, heated, defends him. His master had the power to make them happy or unhappy, to make their work light or burdensome, a pleasure or a toil. That power lay in words and looks and small things, and the happiness he gave was as great as if it had cost a fortune.

Then Scrooge falls quiet. He says he would like to say a word or two to his own clerk just now.
lesson: As someone's boss, you shape a large part of their daily happiness, mostly through small things that cost little. Use that power generously.
people: Mr. Fezziwig, young Ebenezer Scrooge, Dick Wilkins, the Ghost of Christmas Past
source: Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol, Stave 2
